ACTION: ADD 
TITLE:  KernelSHAP Analysis for High-Dimensional Data Sets
PROPOSAL: We analyze the sample complexity of KernelSHAP and its relation to the number of features in the input data. We will use a dataset like MNIST, ImageNet, or a real-world dataset with high-dimensional features such as the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and explore how the number of features affects the sample efficiency of KernelSHAP. By understanding the sample complexity of KernelSHAP in high-dimensional settings, we can better assess when to use this estimator and when to resort to alternative methods such as LeverageSHAP.
CONTROLS: We will compare the results of KernelSHAP to those of LeverageSHAP on the same dataset, using the same number of samples, and measure their respective performance using metrics like Silhouette Coefficient and Calinski-Harabasz Index.
COST: 333.8623 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the performance of KernelSHAP will degrade significantly in high-dimensional settings, and its sample complexity will increase exponentially with the number of features, likely leading to lower quality explanations. This could be mitigated by using more samples but it may also lead to overfitting to the noise in the model's predictions.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Improving Estimators for Shapley Values
PROPOSAL: We explore the idea of pairing KernelSHAP with importance-weighted estimators to improve its sample efficiency and accuracy. We will apply the importance-weighted estimator framework to KernelSHAP, incorporating weights that are proportional to the statistical leverage scores of the subsets in the regression problem. The resulting estimator will be similar in spirit to LeverageSHAP but will leverage the strengths of KernelSHAP's subsampling scheme. We will evaluate the performance of this new estimator on a range of real-world datasets, such as human heart rate variability and stock prices.
CONTROLS: We will also compare the results of our new estimator to those of LeverageSHAP and KernelSHAP, both with and without statistical leverage score weighting.
COST: 1000 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the importance-weighted approach will lead to significant improvements in the accuracy of Shapley value estimates, particularly in high-dimensional settings where KernelSHAP's subsampling scheme can be computationally expensive and may suffer from decreased accuracy. However, the actual performance gains may be capped by the algorithms' sensitivity to the specific problem domain.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Asymptotic Analysis of Unbiased KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Given the disappointing empirical performance of Unbiased KernelSHAP, we aim to formally analyze its asymptotic behavior. We will establish a lower bound on its sample complexity and compare it to that of the original KernelSHAP. By examining the asymptotic limits, we can shed light on why Unbiased KernelSHAP underperformed in practice.
CONTROLS: As a baseline, we will simulate the behavior of KernelSHAP under the same sampling distribution used in Unbiased KernelSHAP.
COST: 1400 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the lower bound will reveal a significant gap in the sample complexity of Unbiased KernelSHAP compared to the original KernelSHAP, contributing to its subpar performance. However, the actual behavior may also depend on other factors such as sampling variability and model parametrization.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: A Multiresolution Analysis of KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We will extend the experiments in KernelSHAP Analysis for High-Dimensional Data Sets by studying the effect of feature hierarchy on the performance of KernelSHAP. We will consider PyTorch Geometric's Citeseer graph as a test case for high dimensional data where there's considerable feature dependencies. By leveraging multiresolution kernels, we can capture both local and global dependencies in the data, leading to more accurate Shapley value estimates.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of KernelSHAP using different types of multiresolution kernels (e.g., Gaussian Processes, Wavelets, or Fourier analysis) to traditional kernel functions.
COST: 600 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the multiresolution approach will significantly improve the performance of KernelSHAP on high-dimensional datasets with underlying graph or spatial structure, allowing for more efficient and accurate Shapley value estimates.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Variance-Based Analysis of Shapley Values
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the variance properties of Shapley values and their estimators, providing a more thorough understanding of their reliability and robustness. By analyzing the variance of the Shapley value estimates, we can better assess the confidence in the attributions provided by these methods.
CONTROLS: We will use Monte Carlo simulations and variance decomposition techniques to analyze the variance of the Shapley values and compare the performance of different estimators (e.g., KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP, and our new importance-weighted estimator).
COST: 1836 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the variance-based analysis will reveal interesting insights into the reliability of Shapley value estimates, potentially leading to new methods or techniques for improving their robustness and accuracy. However, the actual outcomes may depend on the specific problem domain and data characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Theoretical Guarantees for LeverageSHAP
PROPOSAL: We will establish non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for LeverageSHAP, providing a theoretical underpinning for its empirical success. By rigorously analyzing the statistical leverage scores and their impact on the estimation process, we can derive concrete guarantees on the performance of LeverageSHAP in various settings.
CONTROLS: We will compare the theoretical guarantees of LeverageSHAP to those of other estimators (e.g., KernelSHAP, our importance-weighted estimator) and experimentally validate our theoretical findings using real-world datasets.
COST: 2400 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the theoretical guarantees will demonstrate LeverageSHAP's superiority in terms of sample efficiency and estimation accuracy, consistent with its empirical performance. However, the actual outcomes may depend on the problem-specific characteristics and the quality of the input data.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Scalable Shapley Value Estimation for High-Dimensional Data
PROPOSAL: We will explore parallel and distributed computing methods to scale Shapley value estimation to extremely high-dimensional datasets (e.g., millions of features). By harnessing the power of distributed computing, we can apply KernelSHAP or other estimators to large datasets that were previously intractable.
CONTROLS: We will experimentally evaluate the performance of our distributed Shapley value estimation approach using synthetic and real-world datasets with hundreds of thousands to millions of features.
COST: 3600 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that the distributed computing framework will enable Shapley value estimation for extremely high-dimensional data, opening up new possibilities for applications in fields like genomics, computer networks, or image and video processing. However, the actual performance may depend on the specific hardware, software, and data characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Model-Based Shapley Value Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will investigate model-based Shapley value estimation methods, which utilize an underlying model of the data to efficiently estimate Shapley values. By integrating domain knowledge and leveraging model properties, we can develop more accurate and efficient estimation methods.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our model-based Shapley value estimators to state-of-the-art kernel-based methods (e.g., KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP) on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets.
COST: 2880 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that model-based Shapley value estimation methods will offer significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency, especially in domains with complex relationships between features and target variables. However, the actual outcomes may depend on the quality of the underlying model and the specific problem characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Shapley Value Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will explore transfer learning techniques for Shapley value estimation, where we leverage pre-trained models and adapt them to new, related tasks. By transfer learning, we can reduce the need for extensive re-training and improve the efficiency of Shapley value estimation in new domains.
CONTROLS: We will experimentally evaluate the performance of transfer learning for Shapley value estimation using synthetic and real-world datasets, comparing it to traditional re-training methods (e.g., KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP).
COST: 3600 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that transfer learning will significantly reduce the computational overhead of Shapley value estimation, especially when dealing with large datasets or complex models. However, the actual outcomes may depend on the availability of suitable pre-trained models and the similarity between the source and target tasks.

TITLE: A Unified Framework for Shapley Value Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will develop a unified framework for Shapley value estimation that integrates the insights and techniques from the previous proposals, providing a principled and efficient approach to Shapley value estimation for a wide range of problems. The framework will leverage advanced techniques from machine learning, optimization, and statistics to provide accurate and efficient Shapley value estimates for largescale datasets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our unified framework to state-of-the-art methods (e.g., KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP) on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, evaluating its ability to handle high-dimensional data, complex models, and diverse application domains.
COST: 4321.865 GHz
PREDICTION: We expect that our unified framework will provide a significant breakthrough in the field of Shapley value estimation, enabling efficient and accurate explanations for a wide range of machine learning models and applications. However, the actual outcomes will depend on the feasibility of implementing the framework, the availability of computational resources, and the quality of the input data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Current Capabilities for Temporal Change Description
PROPOSAL: This experiment assesses the performance of the current state-of-the-art models, including Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and diffusion-based image generators, on a real-world dataset for the task of temporal change description. Specifically, we compare the results of several MLLMs (e.g., Visual BERT, Learning-backed Image Captioning) and image generators (e.g., DALL-E, StyleGAN) on two real-world datasets: the UC Merced Land Use Scenes and the ISPRS 2D Semantic Labeling Challenge's satellite image dataset. The evaluation metrics include BLEU, ROUGE, and semantic similarity scores.
CONTROLS: We use the static image captioning baseline as a control to demonstrate the impact of the temporal component. We also implement a naive implementation of long-range temporal reasoning using simple interaction, serving as a baseline for the task.
COST: 3338.623
PREDICTION: We expect to see that while current models can capture some aspects of change, they struggle with accurately describing the long-range dynamics and underlying causes of change observed in satellite images. The naive implementation of long-range temporal reasoning will likely perform better than static image captioning, but worse than state-of-the-art MLLMs and image generators.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Addressing the Temporal Gap in MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We propose an extension to the existing MLLMs, incorporating a temporal encoder that models long-range dynamics in the sequence of satellite images. Specifically, we add a temporal transformer layer to Visual BERT, allowing it to reason about the evolution of the scene over time. We then fine-tune this modified MLLM on the same real-world datasets used in proposal 1, evaluating its performance against the state-of-the-art models.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposal 1, showing the impact of adding a temporal encoder on the task of temporal change description. We also ablate different components of the temporal encoder to understand its contributions. Furthermore, we compare our approach to other methods that have attempted to incorporate temporal information into MLLMs.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the temporal change description task, with our modified MLLM reaching state-of-the-art performance. However, it may struggle to capture the underlying causal narrative of the changes, and its performance may degrade when faced with long periods of non-action (i.e., years with no visible changes).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Harnessing the Power of Temporal Reasoning for Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We incorporate the insights gained from proposals 1 and 2 to develop a new model that leverages temporal reasoning for future satellite image forecasting. Specifically, we build upon the modified MLLM from proposal 2, adding a temporal diffusion module that generates plausible future changes based on the observed trends and dynamics. We then fine-tune this model on the same real-world datasets used in proposals 1 and 2, evaluating its performance against state-of-the-art models for this task.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposal 1, showing the impact of using temporal reasoning on the task of future satellite image forecasting. We also ablate different components of the temporal diffusion module to understand its contributions. Furthermore, we compare our approach to existing methods that use temporal information for this task.
COST: 8295
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the future satellite image forecasting task, with our model reaching state-of-the-art performance. However, it may struggle with long-term consistency and the fine-grained temporal semantic interaction between the scene's history and its future evolution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Temporal Consistency through Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial training scheme to improve the temporal consistency of our model from proposal 3. Specifically, we introduce a discriminator that measures the coherence between the generated future image and the historical context. We then train the generator and discriminator simultaneously, forcing the generator to produce temporal consistent outputs. We evaluate the impact of this approach on the future satellite image forecasting task using the same real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposal 3, showing the impact of adversarial training on temporal consistency. We also ablate different components of the adversarial training scheme to understand its contributions. Furthermore, we compare our approach to other methods that use adversarial training for this task.
COST: 10649.4129
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in temporal consistency, with our model outperforming proposal 3 on this aspect. However, the adversarial training may add computational overhead, and its effectiveness may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Forecast Quality using Temporally-Informed Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose a new set of evaluation metrics that specifically focus on the temporal consistency and accuracy of the generated future satellite images. These metrics include a Temporally-Informed Structural Similarity Index (Ti-SSIM) and a Temporally-Informed Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (Ti-PSNR). We evaluate the performance of our model from proposal 4 using these new metrics, and compare it to traditional image quality metrics.
CONTROLS: We use the same real-world datasets as proposals 1-4, and compare our results to those of proposal 4 to demonstrate the effectiveness of the new metrics.
COST: 12615
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the new metrics provide a more nuanced and accurate evaluation of the forecast quality, highlighting the importance of temporal consistency in addition to traditional image quality metrics. However, the design and tuning of these metrics may require additional effort and expertise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncovering the Causal Narrative of Change
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach that explicitly models the causal narrative of change in the scene, using a probabilistic graphical model to represent the relationships between the scene's attributes and the observed changes. We then integrate this model with the temporal reasoning framework from proposal 3, allowing it to better reason about the underlying causes of change and generate more accurate descriptions of the scene's evolution.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposals 3 and 1, showing the impact of modeling the causal narrative on the task of temporal change description. We also ablate different components of the graphical model to understand its contributions.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the accuracy and depth of the change descriptions, with our model able to uncover the underlying causal narrative of the scene's evolution. However, the design and parameterization of the graphical model may require additional expertise and effort.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Harnessing the Power of Temporal Reasoning for Forecasting with Causal Narrative
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal 3, integrating the causal narrative model from proposal 6 into the temporal reasoning framework. This allows the model to better reason about the underlying causes of change and generate more accurate and temporally consistent forecasts. We then fine-tune this revised model on the same real-world datasets used in proposals 1-6, evaluating its performance against state-of-the-art models for this task.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposal 3, showing the impact of incorporating the causal narrative model on the task of future satellite image forecasting. We also ablate different components of the revised model to understand its contributions.
COST: 14120
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the accuracy and temporally consistency of the forecasts, with our revised model outperforming proposal 3 on this task. However, the integration of the causal narrative model may add complexity to the revision, and its effectiveness may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Uncertainty Estimation into the Forecasting Model
PROPOSAL: We propose an extension to the revised temporal reasoning framework from proposal 7, incorporating uncertainty estimation into the forecasting model. Specifically, we use Monte Carlo dropout to estimate the uncertainty of the model's predictions, providing a measure of the confidence in the generated forecasts. We then evaluate the impact of incorporating uncertainty estimation on the task of future satellite image forecasting, using the same real-world datasets and metrics as proposals 1-7.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposal 7, showing the impact of incorporating uncertainty estimation on the task of future satellite image forecasting. We also ablate different components of the uncertainty estimation module to understand its contributions.
COST: 16720
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the accuracy and robustness of the forecasts, with our model better able to capture the uncertainty and variability of real-world satellite image data. However, the incorporation of uncertainty estimation may add computational overhead and require additional tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data-Efficient Training of the Forecasting Model
PROPOSAL: We propose a data-efficient training approach for the revised temporal reasoning framework from proposal 7, using a combination of transfer learning, curriculum learning, and domain adaptation techniques to improve the model's performance on the task of future satellite image forecasting with limited training data. We then evaluate the impact of the proposed approach on the task, using a limited subset of the real-world datasets and metrics as proposals 1-7.
CONTROLS: We compare our results to those of proposal 7, showing the impact of the proposed data-efficient training approach on the task of future satellite image forecasting. We also ablate different components of the approach to understand its contributions.
COST: 19000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the accuracy and robustness of the forecasts, even with limited training data. However, the proposed approach may require additional tuning of hyperparameters and domain-specific adjustments to optimize the results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: System Integration and Real-World Deployment
PROPOSAL: We propose a comprehensive system integration and real-world deployment plan for the forecasting model developed in proposals 1-8. Specifically, we will integrate the model with existing satellite image processing and analysis pipelines, develop a user-friendly interface for forecasting and change description, and conduct a thorough evaluation of the system's performance in real-world settings.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our system to existing satellite image analysis and forecasting systems, and assess the impact of the proposed system on real-world decision-making processes.
COST: 23328
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the accuracy and robustness of the forecasts, and a positive impact on real-world decision-making processes. However, the system integration and deployment may require additional resources and effort, and may be sensitive to changes in the underlying satellite image data and analysis pipelines.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Distribution Shift in Traffic Flow Data
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a pre-trained traffic flow forecasting model, trained on historical data from a specific city, on two datasets: a similar city's data and a different city's data. This will help us understand how well a model generalizes to new datasets and what factors contribute to distribution shift.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline of using a model trained on each city's data individually, and a model using only a few months of data from the test city to simulate a sudden change.
COST: 333.8623
PREDICTION: We expect the pre-trained model to perform significantly better on the similar city's data, but poorly on the different city's data, highlighting the distribution shift issue. The baseline models will likely perform well on their respective datasets but poorly on the other city's data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model Adaptation with Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning for adapting a pre-trained model to a new dataset with distribution shift. Use a pre-trained model trained on a large traffic flow dataset, and fine-tune it on a smaller dataset from a different city or time period. Compare to a baseline of retraining a model from scratch on the new dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare to the model from proposal 1, and a model that only updates the final prediction layer of the pre-trained model.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect the fine-tuned model to perform significantly better than the retrained model, and the model that only updates the final prediction layer will show some improvement but not as much.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Model Adaptation with Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 2 by incorporating an additional control: a model that updates only the model's parameters that are most relevant to the difference in distribution between the source and target datasets. Use a method such as adversarial training or Wasserstein GANs to identify these parameters. Compare to the baseline of retraining a model from scratch on the new dataset.
CONTROLS: Retraining from scratch, fine-tuning the entire model, fine-tuning with the additional adaptation component, and the model that only updates the final prediction layer.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: We expect the adapted model to perform significantly better than the retrained model, and the model that updates only the most relevant parameters will show further improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Ensemble Methods for Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of online ensemble methods that combine the predictions of multiple models, each trained on a different subset of the data or with different architectures, to adapt to distribution shift. Use a variety of methods such as online bagging, boosting, or stacking, and compare to a baseline of using a single model.
CONTROLS: Compare to the model from proposal 2, a baseline of using a single model trained on the entire dataset, and an ensemble of static models trained on the data before the distribution shift.
COST: 933.8
PREDICTION: We expect the online ensemble methods to be effective in adapting to distribution shift, particularly when combined with transfer learning or model adaptation techniques.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Online Ensemble Methods for Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 3 by incorporating an additional control: a incremental learning method that adds new data points to a fixed-size buffer and updates the ensemble based on the new data in each iteration. Compare to the baseline of using a static ensemble and the online ensemble method of proposal 3.
CONTROLS: Static ensemble, online ensemble, incremental learning, and a baseline of using a single model.
COST: 1064.94129
PREDICTION: We expect the incremental learning method to be effective in handling concept drift and adapting to changing distributions, while also being more efficient in terms of computational resources than the online ensemble method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Memory-Augmented Model for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a memory-augmented model that incorporates a neural memory component to store and retrieve relevant information from past time steps, allowing the model to adapt to distribution shift and concept drift. Use a variety of memory architectures such as NASalsy or Ordered Neighbourhood Memory and compare to a baseline of using a traditional LST or GRU.
CONTROLS: Compare to the models from proposals 1, 2, and 3, as well as a baseline of using a traditional LST or GRU.
COST: 1332
PREDICTION: We expect the memory-augmented model to be effective in handling concept drift and adapting to changing distributions, particularly in domains with high noise and variability such as traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Model Adaptation with Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 2 by incorporating an additional component that adapts the pre-trained model to the new distribution using a feedback mechanism that selectively updates the model's parameters based on the performance on a small validation set. Compare to the baseline of retraining a model from scratch on the new dataset.
CONTROLS: Retraining from scratch, fine-tuning the entire model, fine-tuning with the additional adaptation component, and the model that only updates the final prediction layer.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect the adapted model to perform significantly better than the retrained model, and the selective update mechanism will help to reduce overfitting and improve robustness to distribution shift.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial training framework that trains a generator to produce data that can fool a discriminator, which is a time series forecasting model, into making incorrect predictions. Use the generated data to update the model's parameters and adapt to distribution shift. Compare to a baseline of using a static model and a traditional online learning method.
CONTROLS: Compare to the models from proposals 1, 2, 3, and 4, as well as a baseline of using a static model and a traditional online learning method.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect the adversarial training method to be effective in adapting to distribution shift and improving robustness to concept drift, particularly in domains with high noise and variability such as traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Kernel-Based Online Learning for Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Develop a kernel-based online learning method that maps the input data into a high-dimensional feature space using a kernel function, allowing the model to adapt to distribution shift and concept drift. Compare to a baseline of using a traditional online learning method and a kernel-based method with a fixed kernel.
CONTROLS: Compare to the models from proposals 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, as well as a baseline of using a traditional online learning method and a kernel-based method with a fixed kernel.
COST: 1835
PREDICTION: We expect the kernel-based online learning method to be effective in handling high-dimensional input data and adapting to concept drift, particularly in domains with high noise and variability such as traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Time Series Forecasting with Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-task learning framework that trains a single model to perform multiple time series forecasting tasks with different distribution shifts. Use a technique such as task clustering or task pairing to learn shared representations across tasks and adapt to distribution shift. Compare to a baseline of training separate models for each task and a traditional online learning method.
CONTROLS: Compare to the models from proposals 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, as well as a baseline of training separate models for each task and a traditional online learning method.
COST: 2168.1
PREDICTION: We expect the multi-task learning method to be effective in adapting to multiple distribution shifts and improving robustness to concept drift, particularly in domains with high noise and variability such as traffic flow forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Hybrid Retrieval for Multimodal Visual Document Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a hybrid retrieval system combining a ColPali-based vision-centric retriever with a strong dense text retriever (BM25 or sparse lexical representations) on a real-world visual document retrieval benchmark (e.g., MSR-Dracnary, Google-Seq2Seq-Touchdown). Metrics include Mean Average Precision (MAP), Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG), and online latency. Controls include the ColPali-based retriever alone and hybrid retrieval with a weaker text retriever.
CONTROLS: ColPali-based retriever alone, hybrid with a weaker text retriever (e.g., Ancestral CNN)
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The hybrid system should improve MAP and NDCG over the ColPali-based retriever, potentially at the cost of increased latency, but outperform the hybrid with a weaker text retriever. Latency might hinder the system's practicality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lightweight Dense Text Retriever for Efficient Hybrid Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Implement a lightweight dense text retriever (e.g., using a small pre-trained language model or a knowledge distillation approach) that can be combined with a strong vision-centric retriever (ColPali-based) in a hybrid retrieval system. Evaluate the lightweight text retriever's performance on real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks. Compare its performance to a strong but resource-intensive text retriever (e.g., a large pre-trained language model).
CONTROLS: Strong text retriever (e.g., large pre-trained language model like ColBERT), no text retriever
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: The lightweight dense text retriever should achieve a good trade-off between performance and online latency, potentially close to the strong text retriever but with significantly reduced computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Aggregation Methods for Hybrid Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Compare different aggregation methods for combining the output of a vision-centric retriever (ColPali-based) and a dense text retriever in a hybrid retrieval system. Evaluate techniques such as weighted sum, late interaction, or attention-based methods. Assess their impact on performance, online latency, and index memory usage on real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Graded suppression (as a baseline), no aggregation
COST: 7342
PREDICTION: The aggregation methods should provide a way to leverage the strengths of both retrievers, potentially improving performance over a single retriever or hybrid with no aggregation. However, some methods might introduce substantial latency or increase memory usage, potentially hindering the system's practicality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Document and Query Representation Alignment for Hybrid Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Investigate alignment techniques to reduce heterogeneity in the document and query representations used by different retrievers in a hybrid system. Experiment with projection methods, adversarial training, or other techniques to bring the representations of the ColPali-based retriever and the dense text retriever to a common space. Evaluate the impact of these alignment methods on performance, online latency, and index memory usage on real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks.
CONTROLS: No alignment method, random initialization
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: Representation alignment should help the hybrid system to better combine the signals from the vision-centric retriever and the dense text retriever, potentially improving performance over a hybrid system without alignment or the single retrievers. However, some alignment methods might be computationally expensive or introduce additional latency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Studying the Modality Gap in Visual Document Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Conduct an empirical study to quantify the modality gap between vision-centric and text-based representations of documents and queries in visual document retrieval. Measure the performance drop when using a text-based retriever on documents with rich visual content, and vice versa. Analyze the results to identify potential causes of the modality gap and its impact on hybrid retrieval systems. Use real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks and data from existing datasets (e.g., MSR-Dracnary).
CONTROLS: Text-based retriever on vision-centric documents, vision-centric retriever on text-based documents
COST: 10649.4129
PREDICTION: The modality gap will likely be significant, with text-based retrievers struggling with documents containing rich visual content and vice versa. This study will provide insights into the challenges faced by hybrid retrieval systems and inform the development of more effective methods to bridge the modality gap.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Document and Query Representation Alignment for Hybrid Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel attention-based alignment mechanism to reduce heterogeneity in the document and query representations used by different retrievers in a hybrid system. Train an attention network to selectively weight and combine the features from the ColPali-based retriever and the dense text retriever, allowing the representations to adapt to each other dynamically. Evaluate the impact of this alignment method on performance, online latency, and index memory usage on real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks.
CONTROLS: Random initialization, zero-weighted combination
COST: 10690
PREDICTION: The attention-based alignment method should provide a flexible way to combine the strengths of both retrievers, potentially improving performance over a hybrid system without alignment or the single retrievers. However, it might also introduce additional latency and memory requirements due to the dynamic attention weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Tips for Deploying Hybrid Retrieval Systems in Production
PROPOSAL: Investigate the practical aspects of deploying hybrid retrieval systems in production environments. Evaluate factors such as index size, query latency, and system complexity for different hybrid retrieval configurations. Provide recommendations for optimizing the performance and scalability of hybrid retrieval systems, including techniques for reducing index size, improving query efficiency, and simplifying system maintenance. Use real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks and data from existing datasets.
CONTROLS: Single retriever (ColPali-based) deployment, non-hybrid system
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: This study will provide valuable insights into the practical considerations of deploying hybrid retrieval systems in production and offer actionable advice for improving their performance and scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Retrieval for Visual Document Retrieval with Adaptive Indexing
PROPOSAL: Propose an adaptive indexing technique for hybrid retrieval systems that adjusts the index structure in response to changing query patterns and document collections. Evaluate the impact of adaptive indexing on query latency, system complexity, and index size for different hybrid retrieval configurations. Use real-world visual document retrieval benchmarks and data from existing datasets.
CONTROLS: Fixed indexing, standard hybrid retrieval system
COST: 14000
